title: Airfoil Terminology 21
description:
Title: "Effect of altitude on aircraft fuel efficiency"

Summary: The figure presents data on the relationship between altitude and fuel efficiency for various aircraft models. It shows that as altitude increases, so does fuel efficiency up to a certain point after which it starts to decrease. This is important for understanding how atmospheric conditions affect aircraft performance and the potential impact on flight operations.

Visible Labels:
- "NACA report number XYZ"
- "Drag coefficient (Cd)"
- "Lift coefficient (Cl)"
- "Mach number"

Engineering Concepts:
- "Drag coefficient": A measure of the resistance encountered by an aircraft when moving through air. It is a dimensionless quantity that relates the weight of an aircraft to its forward speed relative to air pressure and temperature.
- "Lift coefficient": The ratio of lift (the upward force exerted on an aircraft) to the aircraft's frontal area, characterized by the pressure difference across the wings. It is also dimensionless.
- "Mach number": A dimensionless quantity that represents the ratio of an object's speed to the speed of sound in a particular medium, such as air. In this context, it relates to the altitude at which the aircraft is operating.

Relationships: The figure illustrates how altitude affects both drag and lift coefficients of various aircraft models. As altitude increases, the drag coefficient generally decreases up to a certain point, but then starts to increase again. This decrease in drag is attributed to the thinner air at higher altitudes which reduces air resistance. However, beyond a certain altitude, the drag coefficient increases due to the increased speed and corresponding effects on turbulence and aircraft surface heating. The lift coefficients exhibit similar behavior, with a general trend of increasing with altitude but then decreasing again after a peak point. This is because as altitude increases, air density (and thus lift) generally decreases. The relationships shown in the figure are critical for understanding how changes in altitude affect aircraft performance and can be used to optimize flight routes or design more efficient aircraft for specific operating conditions.
